insights.title: The rest of the skill profile beats impact alone by 0.0625
insights.body: This one is a ridge regression over the 12 skill grades in skills.json — not the 64-d MTNN embedding (dim 64 over 12,966 rows, test_recall_at_10 0.846), which shares the corpus and nothing else. The question the file asks is whether a season's skill profile predicts next season's impact beyond what this season's impact already predicts. Last season's impact grade — skills.json's twelfth skill, labelled 'Two-Way Impact', the same column the trajectory axis averages to get delivery — carries a persistence correlation of 0.4514, and a ridge handed only that one column reproduces it exactly: 0.4514. Handed all twelve grades the ridge reaches 0.5138, and the file records the gain as +0.0625. The split is temporal — train on target season ≤ 2019, test strictly after, 7,706 train pairs against 2,290 test pairs — so the fit is never shown a season that comes after one it is scored on. Sweeping the cut year across 2010, 2013, 2016, 2019 and 2022 leaves the gain positive at all five, mean +0.0559, smallest +0.0488 at the 2022 cut and largest +0.0625 at 2019 — which is also the cut where persistence alone is weakest (0.4514, against 0.4795 at 2022). The null keeps the target and the impact column intact and shuffles only the other eleven grades, 60 reps: mean -0.0007, sd 0.0012, 95th percentile 0.0012, p = 0.000 for the real gain. And 112 of the 10,108 consecutive-season pairs were excluded as merged names, leaving 9,996, because vectors.json has no player identity key — its `id` is a row index and LeBron James has 23 of them — so a name-keyed pair can join one man's season to a different man's next one across the boundary. An earlier permuted-target null (r = -0.096) survives in the file as history and is explicitly not used: the file calls it degenerate, sd 0.1487 over 40 seeds.

insights.title: After pick 30, the expectation curve flatlines
insights.body: The predicted delivery for pick 1 is 61.6909 and it decays smoothly down to 46.7269 at pick 30 — then every pick from 31 to 60 that has a career in this file shares the identical predicted value 45.0642, as do the stray 75, 154 and 160 entries (pick 59 has no careers at all). Undrafted players get 44.3252. So the model's own expectation says the difference between the 31st pick and the 57th pick is exactly zero, and the difference between the last pick in the draft and going undrafted is 0.7390. Manu Ginobili at 57 and Nikola Jokic at 41 are graded against the same number.
insights.source: C:/Users/jcdav/vector-unified/data/trajectory_axis.json → careers[].predicted grouped by careers[].overall / careers[].undrafted (32 distinct slot keys map to 45.0642); report.expectation = 'pedigree.json expect_slot (rookie-scale curve)'

insights.title: Draft capital predicts playing time better than it predicts quality
insights.body: On the matched fantasy-VOR construct over 1,503 drafted players, the correlation between draft expectation and 5-year VOR total is 0.4918 — nearly double the 0.2611 the same draft slot manages against per-season delivery quality. Expected VOR falls off a cliff by bucket: 18.19 for lottery (359 drafted), 6.21 for late-1st (404), 3.05 for early-2nd (375), 1.59 for late-2nd (365). The mechanism shows up in the attrition column: 0.6% of lottery picks never played, versus 22.7% of early-2nd and 48.8% of late-2nd.

insights.title: Over-delivering and still rising are different axes
insights.body: The direction axis scores 566 careers and splits them 114 rising (D0) / 114 declining (D1) / 338 unlabelled, with 287 more dropped for never clearing replacement level at all and 650 for too few seasons. It is built to be independent of the over/under-delivery axis: Jokic is simultaneously T1 (residual +49.1176 against his pick-41 expectation) and D0 (first-half VOR 21.87, second-half 34.52, delta +12.65), while Brook Lopez is a positive-residual career (+16.2428 off a pick-10 bar) that is also D1 (11.39 → 1.13, delta -10.27). The file's own orthogonality note says the earlier single-axis encoding made that combination inexpressible.

insights.title: A same-name defect, and a test that was documented as definitive and wasn't
insights.body: The operator reported on 2026-08-03 that Jaren Jackson and Jaren Jackson Jr. were being combined. The root cause was not suffix stripping: vectors.json carries zero suffixed names across its 12,966 rows, so Sr. and Jr. arrive as one key before this repo sees them, and its `id` field is a row index rather than a player id — LeBron James has 23 of them. There is no player identity key in the source at all. Two tests ran over 2,415 eligible career keys. The arithmetic one — nobody records a season before the year he was drafted — is definitive where it fires, and it fires on exactly one name: `jaren jackson`, earliest draft year 2018 while holding seasons 1996, 1997, 1998, 1999 and 2000 inside a 1996-2025 span. The second test, more than one draft entry for a name (44 names), was DOCUMENTED AS DEFINITIVE AND IS NOT: a drafted player who does not sign can re-enter, and Arvydas Sabonis holds 1985 #77 (voided as underage) and 1986 #24 (Portland) as one person, Wikidata Q297750, born 1964. A Wikidata suffix sweep over all 45 flagged names acquitted 21 of them, confirmed 23 as two or more people, and got no answer for 1 (`greg anderson`), which stays excluded because no evidence is not evidence of one person — leaving an exclusion set of 24. The sweep is required because label matching is exact: asking for 'Glen Rice' never returns Glen Rice Jr. (Q4811246, born 1991), so a bare query reports one person and would clear a genuine father/son pair. Several acquittals are exactly that shape read the other way — the `patrick ewing` key carries picks 1985 #1 and 2008 #43 but only seasons 1996-2001, and `glen rice` carries 1989 #4 and 2013 #35 over seasons 1996-2003; the 18-42 age band leaves one plausible person for each. Downstream, 24 names are excluded from the VOR table, 15 careers are dropped from the trajectory axis as merged, and 112 consecutive-season pairs are dropped from the forward model.

game.prompt: Which player out-delivered his draft slot by more?
game.axis_label: Residual — career delivery minus what the draft slot predicted
game.explainer: Delivery is a player's mean percentile-within-season impact grade across his charted career (0-100). Predicted is what the fitted rookie-scale curve says a player taken at that slot should grade. Residual is delivery minus predicted, so +40 means the career came in 40 percentile points above what the pick was worth — where you were drafted moves the bar, not the grade.

rounds.reveal: Same draft slot, same 50.0633 bar. Malone graded 93.625 across his 8 charted seasons; Bryant graded 83.947 across 19. Delivery is a career mean, so the extra seasons pull his average down.

Butler actually graded higher — 85.533 to VanVleet's 85.111 — but Butler was held to a pick-30 bar of 46.7269 while VanVleet's undrafted bar was 44.3252, and that 2.4016 handicap flips the result. Both carry the T1 label.
The model has no idea who is famous. Hauser's 5 charted seasons grade 84.000 against an undrafted bar of 44.3252; Brunson's 8 grade 82.875 against 45.0642. Both carry the T1 label.
Leonard grades 95.077 over 13 seasons against a 49.3317 bar; Mitchell grades 94.444 over 9 against a slightly steeper 50.0633. Two draft slots of separation, 1.3641 of residual.

Curry was picked eight slots earlier and still wins: 89.625 delivery against a 53.3776 bar beats Giannis's 82.923 against 49.3317. Neither is labelled T1 — of the 99 T1 careers, 61 were picked 31st or later and 31 went undrafted, leaving only 7 from the top 30.

The corpus starts at 1996-97, so only 7 of Stockton's seasons are charted — and those late-career seasons still graded 92.857 against a 48.9992 bar, edging Parker's 89.556 over 18 seasons against 46.9393.

The hardest bar in the file is pick 1 at 61.6909 — no slot is graded against a higher number — and James clears it by 28.6569 across 23 charted seasons (delivery 90.348). Green's 70.071 against the flat 45.0642 second-round bar earns the T1 label but a smaller residual.

The last pick in the draft nearly catches a number-one overall. Davis grades 75.857 against the 61.6909 top-pick bar; Thomas grades 58.500 against 45.0642. The gap is 0.7304 — smaller than the 0.7390 the model puts between the 60th pick and going undrafted.

Hornacek's 51.1858 is the largest residual in the file — no career scores above it — off 96.250 delivery over 4 charted seasons, the minimum this axis accepts, against the flat 45.0642 second-round bar. Sabonis grades 93.833 over 6 seasons against a pick-24 bar of 47.4123, and he is only in the file because the Wikidata suffix sweep acquitted him: two draft rows (1985 #77, 1986 #24) flagged the name, and Q297750, born 1964, is one person.

The second and third largest residuals in the file, sixteen draft slots apart and graded against the identical 45.0642 bar that every pick from 31 onward in this file shares. So the entire margin is delivery: Ginobili 94.1875 over 16 charted seasons against Jokic's 94.1818 over 11, a difference of 0.0057. Both carry the T1 label.

caveat: From the model's own artifact (trajectory_axis.json → caveat_survivorship): "A high pick who never earned 4 charted seasons is ABSENT, not labelled T0. The worst busts leave the league before they accumulate a career, so T0 is biased toward players who under-delivered while still being good enough to keep playing. This understates the tail it is trying to name." The same file's caveat_scope adds: "hoops only. gridiron has the inputs but no exported artifact; pitch has none." 1,107 careers were dropped from the axis for having too few seasons and 15 more as merged careers — names that provably cover more than one person, which merged_careers.json says should be excluded rather than split, because "splitting without an identity key is a guess dressed as a repair." The forward model carries its own refusal: hoops_forward_report.json notes that the tennis version of the same question finds +0.0941 over a 0.7486 persistence baseline, and says the two gains are not directly comparable — different targets, different baselines, different sports.
